title: Shortest Bridge
prompt: You are given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid` containing exactly two islands (each a group of `1`s connected 4-directionally, and the two islands are not connected to each other). You may change `0`s to `1`s to connect the two islands into a single island. Return the minimum number of `0`s you must flip to connect them (equivalently, the length of the shortest bridge between the two islands).

examples.explanation: The two single-cell islands are diagonal neighbors; flipping either of the two adjacent 0s connects them with a bridge of length 1.
The two islands are two cells apart in Manhattan distance minus the endpoints, requiring 2 flips to connect.
The two single-cell islands sit at opposite corners of the grid, requiring the maximum possible bridge length for this small grid size.

constraints: There are exactly two islands in grid
hints: First find one full island using DFS/BFS flood-fill, and mark all of its cells so they're distinguishable from the other island.

Do a multi-source BFS starting from every cell of the first island simultaneously, expanding outward through water; the first time you touch a cell belonging to the second island, the number of expansion steps taken is the answer.
This is like walls-and-gates or rotting-oranges: distance grows level by level, so BFS (not DFS) guarantees the first contact with the second island is via the shortest possible bridge.

solution.approach: First locate the two islands: DFS flood-fill from any land cell to identify all cells of 'island A', collecting them into a BFS queue and marking them visited. Then run multi-source BFS from that entire queue simultaneously, expanding into water cells one ring at a time and counting the number of expansion steps. The first time the BFS wave reaches a cell that is land (part of the second island), the number of steps taken to get there is exactly the minimum bridge length, since BFS explores in strictly increasing distance order.
